tagline: Product security for the software you ship — self-hosted

site.title: Matelot — product security, DevSecOps and CRA compliance, self-hosted in your cluster
site.description: SBOMs, vulnerability correlation, policies and gates, keyless registries, managed runners and CRA evidence. One Helm chart, one cell per organization, in your own Kubernetes cluster.

hero.title:
Know what you ship,
prove it is secure
hero.subtitle: Matelot keeps a live picture of every product, service, release and deployment: what is in it, which vulnerabilities reach production, which policies apply, and the evidence the Cyber Resilience Act expects. It runs in your own Kubernetes cluster from one Helm chart, so your code, SBOMs and findings never leave your infrastructure.

metrics.label: per organization: your cluster, your database, your identity realm
plus one Helm chart — signed, with SBOM attestations, pulled from GitHub Packages
stored for keyless registry access on AWS, Azure and Google

pillars.title: Every release has a bill of materials
pillars.body: Repositories, builds, releases, container images and deployments form one graph. The security pipeline generates an SBOM per release, correlates it with vulnerability intelligence continuously, and tells you which products, versions and environments a CVE really affects — and whether production is exposed.
pillars.alt: Abstract visual for inventory and SBOM

pillars.title: Decide once, enforce everywhere
pillars.body: Policies live at the organization, workspace, team or project and inherit downward. Pipelines evaluate them as gates; deployments can be rejected on the same rules. Exceptions are explicit, owned and time-limited. Service coverage shows which services still lack a repository, a recent scan, an SBOM, a policy or a recorded deployment.
pillars.alt: Abstract visual for policies and gates

pillars.title: Compliance as a by-product of shipping
pillars.body: Each release gets a signed evidence bundle: what shipped, what was known, what was decided, what was enforced, where it ran. CRA readiness checks name the requirement each gap maps to. The audit trail records every change with who, what and why — in a database you operate.

items.title: Security pipeline
items.body: Checkout, SBOM, secrets, IaC, SAST and dependency scanning as one pipeline per service, with a policy gate at the end. Run it from the UI, the CLI or your CI.

items.title: Vulnerability and risk
items.body: Findings correlated against SBOMs and deployments; risk scored by CVSS, exploitation, exposure and criticality. The same CVE is Medium in development and Critical when internet-facing in production.

items.title: Keyless registries
items.body: Pull from and push to ECR, ACR and Artifact Registry with workload identity federation — the cell holds no long-lived registry secrets. Docker Hub, GHCR and any v2 registry work with tokens.

items.title: Managed and self-hosted runners
items.body: Every cell ships managed runners inside the cluster, so pipelines run on day one. Add your own runner pools for private networks and other clusters; jobs are routed by tags and pools.

items.title: Remediation and SLAs
items.body: A fix-first queue ordered by risk, SLA clocks per severity, owners, and issues created in GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket or Jira with status kept in sync.

items.title: CLI, CI tokens and MCP
items.body: Every action in the UI is a `matelot` command. CI authenticates with signed, scoped tokens — never bearer secrets. The MCP server lets an AI assistant query the platform with your permissions.

items.title: Hierarchical RBAC and audit
items.body: Organization → workspace → team → project → service → environment, with roles that inherit downward, SSO through the cell's own Keycloak, and an audit trail on every mutation.

items.title: Built to be operated by you
items.body: One Helm chart installs the whole cell. Scheduled backups to a volume and your S3 bucket, a tested restore path, upgrades that roll only the application pods, usage per month, and a CLI for everything.

integrations.title: Connects to what you already run
integrations.body: Only what exists today — nothing on this list is a roadmap item.

items.a: Yes, only. You install a cell in your own Kubernetes cluster with one Helm chart (`helm install … oci://ghcr.io/matelot-io/charts/secops-cell`). The cell contains everything: API, worker, web app, managed runners, a container registry, Postgres, Redis and Keycloak. There is no hosted edition and no component that calls home.

items.q: What do I need to run it?
items.a: A Kubernetes 1.28+ cluster with an ingress controller, TLS (cert-manager or your own certificates), a default StorageClass and about 2 vCPU / 5 GiB for a small cell. The install guide lists the values that matter; everything else has a documented default.

In the cell: your cluster, your region, your database. Backups go to a volume in the cell and, if you want, to an S3-compatible bucket you own. Nothing leaves the cell except the integrations you connect (your Git host, registries, issue tracker, chat).

No. Matelot is closed source. Customers receive the container images and the Helm chart; both are published on GitHub Packages, signed with cosign (keyless, GitHub OIDC) and carry SBOM attestations, so you can verify what you run with the same tools Matelot uses on your software.

items.q: How does keyless registry access work?
items.a: The cell has an OIDC issuer. AWS, Azure and Google trust it through workload identity federation, so the platform exchanges short-lived identity tokens for registry access and stores no long-lived credentials. Token-based registries (Docker Hub, GHCR, any v2 registry) are supported too, with the secret encrypted at rest in your database.

items.q: What do you mean by CRA evidence?
items.a: For each release the platform produces a signed bundle with the SBOM, the known vulnerabilities at the time, the decisions and exceptions, the policies that were enforced and where the release ran. CRA readiness checks name the requirement each gap maps to, so you know what is missing before an audit does.

items.q: Do I need to run my own runners?
items.a: No. Every cell ships managed runners inside the cluster, so pipelines run on day one. Add self-hosted runner pools when jobs must reach private networks or other clusters; jobs are routed by pool and tags.

items.q: How do pipelines fit into my CI?
items.a: Your CI calls the matelot CLI with a signed, scoped CI token — never a bearer secret. Examples for GitHub Actions, GitLab CI and Bitbucket Pipelines are in the docs. Deployments are recorded the same way, and policies can reject them.

Per user and month, in three tiers: Free for small teams, Premium and Ultimate billed annually. The prices on this page are indicative until the first commercial release. No licence key is needed to install today; entitlements arrive with the commercial release and existing cells keep working.

Each release publishes the four images and the chart at the same version. `helm upgrade` with the new chart version rolls only the application pods; the database, Keycloak, Redis and the registry keep running. Release notes with image digests are on GitHub.

items.q: Can an AI assistant use it?
items.a: Yes. The MCP server exposes the API as tools, authenticated with your personal token and limited by your permissions; read-only tokens stay read-only. Claude Desktop and Claude Code snippets are generated by `matelot mcp`.
